title: Motive is generally distinct from tortious liability

content.overview: Motive is generally distinct from tortious liability. A lawful act does not ordinarily become actionable merely because it was done with an improper motive, although malice is legally material in particular torts.
content.glance: Motive is generally distinct from tortious liability. A lawful act does not ordinarily become actionable merely because it was done with an improper motive, although malice is legally material in particular torts.
content.study: Motive is generally distinct from tortious liability. A lawful act does not ordinarily become actionable merely because it was done with an improper motive, although malice is legally material in particular torts.\n\nCommon law separates the legal character of an act from the reason why it was done. Bradford Corporation v Pickles is the classic example. By contrast, malicious prosecution requires malice and absence of reasonable and probable cause. The court therefore identifies the tort first and asks whether motive or malice is an ingredient.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Common law separates the legal character of an act from the reason why it was done. Bradford Corporation v Pickles is the classic example. By contrast, malicious prosecution requires malice and absence of reasonable and probable cause. The court therefore identifies the tort first and asks whether motive or malice is an ingredient.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: There is no general statutory rule making bad motive actionable. In malicious prosecution and abuse of process, improper purpose is central. In other torts, motive may be evidentially relevant but cannot replace proof of the substantive elements.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Identify the pleaded tort. 2. Determine whether intention or malice is an ingredient. 3. Do not infer liability from moral disapproval alone. 4. Where relevant, prove malice by direct or circumstantial evidence.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: The civil standard applies. Malice may be inferred from circumstances where the tort requires it. Where motive is legally irrelevant, evidence of spite has limited independent value.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: A pleading based only on bad motive is vulnerable if it discloses no recognised cause of action. The plaint should identify the substantive tort and plead its ingredients. Limitation depends on the underlying cause of action.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Improper motive does not ordinarily convert lawful conduct into a tort; where malice is a defined ingredient it must be proved. The claimant must still prove the remaining ingredients on the civil standard.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Malice is not a universal ingredient of tortious liability. A court should not infer liability from the label alone.
